hops.title: An acorn worm embryo shows part of the vertebrate isthmus signaling pattern
hops.text: Researchers had proposed that signaling centers like the isthmus evolved with the vertebrate brain. In 2012 a team studied embryos of the acorn worm Saccoglossus kowalevskii, a soft mud-burrowing worm with no centralized brain. The embryos switch on Wnt1 just in front of an Fgf8-family gene, in two neighbouring bands around the body at the collar-trunk border. Reducing FGF signaling weakened Engrailed there, and patches with Wnt signaling blocked lacked detectable Engrailed. Lancelets, closer relatives of vertebrates, have an Otx-Gbx seam with no Wnt1 and no localized isthmus-like Fgf8-family band there. The authors propose that lancelets lost an older program; the lancelet data alone would also fit a later origin.

sources.citation: Chandel & Hörnblad, International Journal of Developmental Biology 68:211-222 (2024)

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: An acorn worm with a long, tapered pale pink proboscis and short orange collar emerging from wet tidal mud beside small seashells in shallow seawater.
image.caption: Acorn worm embryos switch on Wnt1 and an Fgf8-family gene side by side at a body border, without a brain.

hops.afterHeading: Take it away: started, then lost
hops.title: The swaying mouse: a cerebellum mutant with brittle bones
hops.text: The spontaneous mouse mutant swaying walks unsteadily because the front of its cerebellum is malformed. In 1991 Kirk Thomas, Mario Capecchi and colleagues traced it to a one-base deletion in Wnt1 predicted to shorten the protein; the defects matched those of a Wnt1 mutant line made by gene targeting. The original reports described the brain and left the skeleton out. In 2013 recessive WNT1 mutations were linked to brittle bone disease in people, and a 2014 study found that swaying mice have fragile, fracture-prone bones. Brain scans of six people with the WNT1 form later showed midbrain and cerebellar abnormalities, including one person with no cerebellum.

sources.citation: Joeng et al., Human Molecular Genetics 23:4035-4042 (2014)
Aldinger et al., Journal of Medical Genetics 53:427-430 (2016)

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A small white mouse leaning slightly off-balance on a wooden rod, with a magnifying glass resting on the bench nearby.
image.caption: A one-base Wnt1 deletion gave swaying mice a malformed cerebellum, and fragile bones found only decades later.

hops.title: Blind cavefish switch on a forebrain Fgf8 source two hours early
hops.text: Blind cavefish, a form of the Mexican tetra Astyanax mexicanus, start building eyes as embryos, but the lower retina is reduced or missing. Earlier signaling at a forebrain organizer may help explain why. At the front of the forebrain, a signaling center switches on Fgf8 about two hours earlier in Pachón cavefish embryos than in sighted river fish. Cell tracking showed that a patch of early neural plate cells helps build the lower retina in river fish and mainly the hypothalamus in cavefish. A brief early block of FGF receptors restored a river-fish gene pattern and, in some embryos, brought back the lower retina.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A sighted silvery river fish and a pale eyeless cavefish swimming beside a small sand hourglass on a stone.
image.caption: In Pachón cavefish, anterior forebrain Fgf8 starts earlier; the embryonic patch forming river-fish lower retina contributes mainly to the hypothalamus.
